modules.comments:
Error-diffusion and ordered dithering, in one import. This module
re-exports what a typical application needs:

- `ditherImage`, which dithers an image in memory; `ditherRows`, which
  dithers a lazy stream of rows, each when it's needed; and
  `initDithering` with `ditherRow`, one row at a time from any source;
- the kernels `floydSteinberg`, `atkinson`, `jarvisJudiceNinke`,
  `stucki`, `burkes`, `sierra3`, `sierra2`, `sierraLite`, `fan`,
  `shiauFan` and `shiauFan2`, and `noDiffusion` for none;
- the quantizers `threshold`, `nearestLevel` with `evenRamp`, and
  `perChannel` for color; `nearestColor` with the palette presets;
  `bayer` and `ordered` for ordered dithering;
- `ditherImageBy`, `ditherRowsBy` and `initDitheringBy`, the same
  with their settings in a `DitherParams`, built from `defaults` with
  `withKernel`, `withGamma` and `withScan` (`raster`, the default, or
  `serpentine`, the rows alternating);
- `ditherImageWith`, `ditherRowsWith` and `initDitheringWith`, the
  same with a gamma curve, `gammaOff`, `gamma1p2`, `gamma1p5`,
  `gamma1p8` or `gammaSrgb`, which says how the stored numbers turn
  into light; and `toGray`, a color's gray by that curve;
- the pixel types `RGB` and `RGBA`, and the types for signatures.

Import it qualified, as names like `threshold` or `c64` are short:

```purescript
import Puregrain as P

dithered = P.ditherImage P.floydSteinberg (P.threshold 128.0) image
```

The building blocks for your own variants (distance metrics, threshold
maps, custom quantizers) are in the modules they come from:
`Puregrain.Palette`, `Puregrain.Ordered`, `Puregrain.Quantize`,
`Puregrain.Pixel`, `Puregrain.Kernel` and `Puregrain.Gamma`. Dithering with cells, as on
the screens of 8-bit machines, is in `Puregrain.Cells` and
`Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum`, outside this module.
modules.name: Puregrain

declarations.comments:
The order the pixels are visited in, for `withScan`: `raster` or
`serpentine`. Opaque.
declarations.title: Scan

declarations.comments:
An image being dithered one row at a time, for `ditherRow`: the
settings, the quantizer, and the error waiting for the rows still to
come; `a` is the pixel type. Opaque.

An immutable value: keep and reuse one, for an undo, say. Dithering a
row from it again redoes that row's work, and no more.
declarations.title: Dithering

declarations.comments:
How an image is dithered, apart from the quantizer: the kernel, where
each pixel's error goes; the gamma, in which light; and the scan, the
order the pixels are visited in. Opaque: start from `defaults` and
change one setting at a time with the `with…` functions, chained with
`#`:

```purescript
params = defaults # withKernel floydSteinberg # withGamma gammaSrgb # withScan serpentine

dithered = ditherImageBy params (threshold 128.0) image
```

The order of the `with…` calls doesn't matter; a later call of the
same one replaces the earlier setting. The quantizer is an argument of
its own, since its type depends on the driver: a `Quantize a` for
`ditherImageBy`, a cell rule for `Puregrain.Cells.ditherCellsBy`.
declarations.title: DitherParams

declarations.comments:
Sets the scan, the order the pixels are visited in.

- `Scan`: `raster`, every row left to right (the default), or
  `serpentine`, the rows alternating.
- `DitherParams`: the settings to change.

Returns the settings with that scan, the others unchanged.
declarations.title: withScan

declarations.comments:
Sets the kernel.

- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes, from `Puregrain.Kernel`;
  `noDiffusion` for nowhere.
- `DitherParams`: the settings to change.

Returns the settings with that kernel, the others unchanged.
declarations.title: withKernel

declarations.comments:
Sets the gamma.

- `Gamma`: how the stored numbers turn into light, from
  `Puregrain.Gamma`: `gammaOff`, `gamma1p2`, `gamma1p5`, `gamma1p8` or
  `gammaSrgb`. Which for which view:
  [docs/gamma.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/gamma.md).
- `DitherParams`: the settings to change.

Returns the settings with that gamma, the others unchanged.
declarations.title: withGamma

declarations.comments:
Serpentine scanning: the rows alternate, the first (row 0) left to
right, the second right to left, and so on, top to bottom. On a row
scanned right to left the kernel is mirrored, so each pixel's error
still goes to pixels not yet processed: an offset's `dx` then counts
to the left. It's the usual remedy for the patterns error diffusion
draws when every row is scanned the same way.

Each pixel's quantizer still gets its own position, counted from the
image's left and top edges, so ordered dithering and machine cells
work as with `raster`. With `noDiffusion` it changes nothing. What it
changes, and what it doesn't:
[docs/error-diffusion.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/error-diffusion.md#serpentine-scanning).
declarations.title: serpentine

declarations.comments: Every row left to right, top to bottom: the default.
declarations.title: raster

declarations.comments:
The state before the first row, for `ditherRow`, with a gamma and a
kernel.

- `a` and `Gamma`: as for `ditherImageWith`.
- `Kernel` and `Quantize a`: as for `initDithering`.

Returns what `initDitheringBy (defaults # withKernel kernel # withGamma
gamma)` returns.
declarations.title: initDitheringWith

declarations.comments:
The state before the first row, for `ditherRow`, with the settings
given.

- `a`, `DitherParams` and `Quantize a`: as for `ditherImageBy`.

Dithers nothing yet; the first row fixes the image's width. `ditherRow`
then gives the same rows as `ditherImageBy`, each as stored values.
declarations.title: initDitheringBy

declarations.comments:
The state before the first row, for `ditherRow`, with a kernel and no
other setting.

- `Kernel` and `Quantize a`: as for `ditherImage`.

Returns what `initDitheringBy (defaults # withKernel kernel)` returns.
declarations.title: initDithering

declarations.comments:
Dithers a lazy stream of rows, with a gamma and a kernel.

- `a` and `Gamma`: as for `ditherImageWith`.
- `Kernel`, `Quantize a`, `LL.List (Array a)`: as for `ditherRows`.

Returns what `ditherRowsBy (defaults # withKernel kernel # withGamma
gamma)` returns.
declarations.title: ditherRowsWith

declarations.comments:
Dithers a lazy stream of rows, with the settings given.

- `a`, `DitherParams` and `Quantize a`: as for `ditherImageBy`.
- `LL.List (Array a)`: the rows, top to bottom, all of the same length;
  the list may be endless.

Returns the dithered rows as a lazy list, the same rows as
`ditherImageBy`. Each row is read and dithered only when its result is
first needed, so only the rows in flight are in memory. At a row whose
length differs from the first row's, it stops with an error naming
the row; the rows before it have come out.
declarations.title: ditherRowsBy

declarations.comments:
Dithers a lazy stream of rows, with a kernel and no other setting.

- `a`, `Kernel` and `Quantize a`: as for `ditherImage`.
- `LL.List (Array a)`: the rows, as for `ditherRowsBy`.

Returns what `ditherRowsBy (defaults # withKernel kernel)` returns.
declarations.title: ditherRows

declarations.comments:
Dithers the next row.

- `Dithering a`: the state, from `initDitheringBy`, `initDithering`,
  `initDitheringWith` or the previous row.
- `Array a`: the row, as long as the first one.

Returns the dithered row and the state for the next one: the same rows
as the matching `ditherImage…`. `Left`, with a message naming the row,
for a row of a different length; the state passed in is untouched, so
you can carry on with a corrected row.
declarations.title: ditherRow

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory, with a gamma and a kernel.

- `a`: as for `ditherImageBy`.
- `Gamma`: how the stored numbers turn into light: `gammaOff`, the
  same as `ditherImage`, or `gamma1p2`, `gamma1p5`, `gamma1p8` or
  `gammaSrgb` (linear light).
- `Kernel`, `Quantize a`, `Array (Array a)`: as for `ditherImage`.

Returns what `ditherImageBy (defaults # withKernel kernel # withGamma
gamma)` returns.

```purescript
ditherImageWith gammaSrgb floydSteinberg (threshold 128.0) image
```
declarations.title: ditherImageWith

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory, with the settings given.

- `a`: the pixel type, `Number` for gray, `RGB` or `RGBA`; any type
  with `Ring`, `Scalable` and `ColorChannels` works.
- `DitherParams`: the kernel, the gamma and the scan, from `defaults`
  and the `with…` functions.
- `Quantize a`: picks each pixel's output value.
- `Array (Array a)`: the image, rows top to bottom, each left to right,
  all of the same length.

Returns the dithered image, all at once, as stored values. Under a
gamma other than `gammaOff`, each row is taken to light, dithered
there, and brought back: the error and the amounts of light (ordered
dithering's patterns) are in light; the choices of the nearest level
or color stay on stored values, as the eye sees them; a level or a
palette color of whole numbers comes back exactly. Stops with an error
naming a row whose length differs from the first row's.

```purescript
ditherImageBy (defaults # withKernel floydSteinberg # withGamma gammaSrgb) (threshold 128.0) image
```
declarations.title: ditherImageBy

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory, with a kernel and no other setting.

- `a`: the pixel type, `Number` for gray, `RGB` or `RGBA`; any type
  with `Ring` and `Scalable` works, `ColorChannels` not needed.
- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes; `noDiffusion` for nowhere.
- `Quantize a`: picks each pixel's output value.
- `Array (Array a)`: the image, as for `ditherImageBy`.

Returns what `ditherImageBy (defaults # withKernel kernel)` returns.
declarations.title: ditherImage

declarations.comments:
The settings to start from, each one neutral: no diffusion
(`noDiffusion`), so each pixel is only quantized; `gammaOff`; and
`raster`, every row left to right. Dithering with them alone is plain
quantizing, or pure ordered dithering with a quantizer from
`Puregrain.Ordered`; add a kernel with `withKernel` for error
diffusion.
declarations.title: defaults

declarations.comments:
A curve between a picture's stored values and light: one of
`Puregrain.Gamma`'s presets, `gammaOff`, `gamma1p2`, `gamma1p5`,
`gamma1p8` and `gammaSrgb`.
declarations.title: Gamma

declarations.comments:
A color's gray, for dithering a color picture in gray.

- `Gamma`: the curve, which decides the formula; give the dithering
  the same one.
- `RGB`: the color, as stored.

Returns the gray as a stored value, 0 to 255. A neutral color, with
red, green and blue equal, gives exactly that value. With `gammaOff`,
the gray is luma, 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B on the stored values, the
classic conversion. With a curve, it's the gray that gives off as much
light as the color: 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B on the channels'
light (luminance, with `gammaSrgb`), brought back to a stored value.
Saturated colors then come out lighter than with luma, pure blue 76
instead of 29 with `gammaSrgb`; natural colors such as skin barely
change.

```purescript
toGray gammaOff (RGB { r: 0.0, g: 0.0, b: 255.0 })    -- 29.07
toGray gammaSrgb (RGB { r: 0.0, g: 0.0, b: 255.0 })   -- 75.96…

ditherImageWith gammaSrgb floydSteinberg (threshold 128.0)
  (map (map (toGray gammaSrgb)) image)
```
declarations.title: toGray

declarations.comments:
Linear light: the sRGB standard's curve (IEC 61966-2-1), a straight
piece near black and a power of 2.4 above it, which behaves much like a
power of 2.2 overall.
declarations.title: gammaSrgb

declarations.comments:
No conversion: the stored numbers are taken as amounts of light, as
dithering has always taken them. The default.
declarations.title: gammaOff

declarations.comments:
A power curve: light = (value / 255)^1.8 × 255, the gamma of Apple
RGB, the classic Macintosh's color space.
declarations.title: gamma1p8

declarations.comments: A power curve: light = (value / 255)^1.5 × 255.
declarations.title: gamma1p5

declarations.comments: A power curve: light = (value / 255)^1.2 × 255.
declarations.title: gamma1p2

declarations.comments:
One neighbour that gets a share of a pixel's error.

- `dx`: columns to the right; negative to the left. With serpentine
  scanning (`Puregrain.Dither.serpentine`), a row scanned right to
  left mirrors the kernel: `dx` then counts to the left.
- `dy`: rows down.
- `weight`: the share of the error.
declarations.title: Offset

declarations.comments:
A checked list of neighbours. Build one with `fromOffsets`, or use a
ready-made one. Opaque, so every kernel `ditherImage` gets is valid.
declarations.title: Kernel

declarations.comments:
Stucki (Peter Stucki, IBM Zurich, 1981): 12 neighbours over the next 2
rows, like Jarvis–Judice–Ninke, with weights that give a clean, sharp
result.
declarations.title: stucki

declarations.comments:
Sierra Lite (Frankie Sierra, 1989–1990; also "Filter Lite" or
"Sierra-2-4A"): 3 neighbours, one fewer than Floyd–Steinberg, for
similar results.
declarations.title: sierraLite

declarations.comments:
Sierra 3 (Frankie Sierra, 1989–1990; also "Sierra" or "three-row
Sierra"): 10 neighbours over the next 2 rows, for results like
Jarvis–Judice–Ninke's with fewer neighbours.
declarations.title: sierra3

declarations.comments:
Sierra 2 (Frankie Sierra, 1989–1990; also "two-row Sierra"): 7
neighbours over the next row, a faster Sierra 3.
declarations.title: sierra2

declarations.comments:
Shiau–Fan 2 (Jeng-Nan Shiau and Zhigang Fan, 1993): the same aim with 5
neighbours, reaching three columns to the left.
declarations.title: shiauFan2

declarations.comments:
Shiau–Fan (Jeng-Nan Shiau and Zhigang Fan, 1993): 4 neighbours, with
weights in eighths, made to reduce the "worm" patterns of
Floyd–Steinberg.
declarations.title: shiauFan
noDiffusion

declarations.comments:
Jarvis–Judice–Ninke (1976): 12 neighbours over the next 2 rows, for
the smoothest texture, at about 2.5 times Floyd–Steinberg's cost.
declarations.title: jarvisJudiceNinke

declarations.comments: Floyd–Steinberg (1976): 4 neighbours, the classic.
declarations.title: floydSteinberg

declarations.comments:
Fan (Zhigang Fan, 1993): Floyd–Steinberg's 4 neighbours with one weight
moved, its 1/16 from below-right to two columns left.
declarations.title: fan

declarations.comments:
Burkes (Daniel Burkes, 1988): Stucki without its last row, so 7
neighbours over the next row: a little less clean, at a lower cost.
declarations.title: burkes

declarations.comments:
Atkinson (Apple, 1980s): 6 neighbours over the next 2 rows, each
getting 1/8, so only 3/4 of the error is passed on: crisper and
higher in contrast, at the cost of detail in dark and light tones.
declarations.title: atkinson

declarations.comments:
A threshold map: a grid of thresholds, each strictly between 0 and 1,
repeated across the image. Build one with `bayer` or
`compileThresholdMap`; opaque, so every map is checked: rectangular
and non-empty.
declarations.title: ThresholdMap

declarations.comments:
Ordered dithering over levels. For a value `v` between two
neighbouring levels `lo` < `hi`, it picks `hi` exactly when
`(v − lo) / (hi − lo)` is above the pixel's threshold, else `lo`.

- `ThresholdMap`: the thresholds, from `bayer` or
  `compileThresholdMap`.
- `NonEmptyArray Number`: the levels, in any order; with 0 and 255,
  classic 1-bit ordered dithering.

A value at a level stays that level; values beyond the lowest or
highest level snap to it, as accumulated error can push them there in
the hybrid with error diffusion. For color, lift it with `perChannel`,
which gives every channel the same position.

With a gamma (`Puregrain.Dither.ditherImageWith`), `v`, `lo` and `hi`
are amounts of light, so each pattern gives off the light it stands
for; levels that aren't whole numbers are rounded first. With few
patterns, such as `bayer 2` over two levels, the darkest grays then
turn black: they're nearer to black's light than to the first
pattern's.
declarations.title: ordered

declarations.comments:
The Bayer threshold map.

- `Int`: the side, a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, …).

`Nothing` for any other side. The thresholds are `(rank + 0.5) / n²`
for side `n` (see `compileThresholdMap`). `bayer 1` is 0.5 everywhere:
`ordered` with it picks the nearer level, like `nearestLevel`.

```purescript
-- pure 1-bit ordered dithering with the 8 × 8 map
map (\m -> ditherImage noDiffusion (ordered m (evenRamp 2)) image) (bayer 8)
```
declarations.title: bayer

declarations.comments:
A quantizer that turns each pixel into the nearest palette color, all
three channels together, by `distance2`; on a tie, the earlier color.

- `NonEmptyArray RGB`: the palette, e.g. from
  `Puregrain.Palette.Presets`.

```purescript
ditherImage floydSteinberg (nearestColor websafe216) image
```

With a gamma (`Puregrain.Dither.ditherImageWith`), the nearest color is
still chosen on stored values, as the eye sees them: each corrected
pixel is brought back from light for the comparison, and the chosen
color taken to light, while the error stays in light. A pixel that's
exactly a byte's light comes back as that byte, so without diffusion
the result is the one `ditherImage` gives.
declarations.title: nearestColor

declarations.comments:
The ZX Spectrum's 15 distinct colors: its 8 (black, blue, red, magenta,
green, cyan, yellow, white) at normal brightness, then the 7 non-black
ones with BRIGHT (bright black is black). Normal is 0xD8 = 216, about
85% of bright, the common model: the real colors were never measured,
and many emulators use 0xD7 or 0xCD instead. This is the per-pixel
palette; for the real machine's 2 colors per 8×8 cell, see
`Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum`.
Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZX_Spectrum_graphic_modes; values as
lospec.com/palette-list/zx-spectrum.
declarations.title: zxSpectrum

declarations.comments:
The 216 "web-safe" colors: every combination of 0, 51, 102, 153, 204
and 255 per channel (a 6×6×6 cube), `r` varying slowest, so it starts
at black and ends at white. Being a complete grid, its nearest color is
the nearest step in each channel separately — the same result as
`perChannel (nearestLevel (evenRamp 6))`.
declarations.title: websafe216

declarations.comments:
The 16-color IBM PC palette, CGA's "RGBI" colors in index order 0–15:
each channel 0x00 or 0xAA, plus an intensity bit adding 0x55, with the
IBM 5153 monitor's brown (color 6 is #AA5500, not dark yellow). Also
EGA's and VGA's defaults and the DOS text colors; the Linux console
uses the same values, in ANSI order. EGA's full 64 colors need no
preset: `perChannel (nearestLevel (evenRamp 4))`.
Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_Graphics_Adapter (RGBI palette).
declarations.title: cga16

declarations.comments:
The Commodore 64's 16 colors, in VIC-II index order: black, white, red,
cyan, purple, green, blue, yellow, orange, brown, light red, dark grey,
grey, light green, light blue, light grey. There's no official RGB
definition; these are Colodore's values, Pepto's model of the VIC-II's
colors (2017), with the display set to brightness 47.5, contrast 100
and saturation 70.
Source: pepto.de/projects/colorvic (the model); the values as in VICE's
data/C64/colodore.vpl, which those settings reproduce exactly.
declarations.title: c64

declarations.comments:
Black, then white. With `nearestColor` it dithers a color image
straight down to pure black and white, choosing by RGB distance —
which isn't brightness: pure green is nearer to black.
declarations.title: blackWhite

declarations.comments:
xterm's 256 colors: `ansi16` (indices 0–15), a 6×6×6 cube (16–231,
index 16 + 36r + 6g + b, levels 0, 95, 135, 175, 215, 255), and 24
grays (232–255, 8 + 10i). 7 cube colors repeat `ansi16` ones, so 249
are distinct; `nearestColor` picks the earlier index of a pair. In a
real terminal the first 16 come from its theme.
Source: xterm's 256colres.pl.
declarations.title: ansi256

declarations.comments:
The 16 ANSI terminal colors as xterm's defaults, in index order: black,
red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white, then the 8 bright ones.
ANSI names the colors but defines no RGB, and terminals differ; the
Linux console's values are `cga16`, in CGA order.
Source: xterm's XTerm-col.ad, matching the xterm column of
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code.
declarations.title: ansi16

children.comments:
Alpha too, like the other channels, as in the `Ring` and `Scalable`
instances.
children.title: <anonymous>

children.comments: Red, green and blue; alpha stays as it is.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A color pixel with alpha: as `RGB`, plus `a`, which error diffusion
treats like the other channels.
declarations.title: RGBA

children.comments: Compared and shown like the record inside.
children.title: <anonymous>

children.comments:
Channel by channel, `mul` and `one` too, though error diffusion uses
only `add`, `zero` and `sub`.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A color pixel: red, green and blue, each from 0 to 255 by convention.
Adds, subtracts and scales channel by channel, as error diffusion
needs.
declarations.title: RGB

declarations.comments:
A gray pixel: one channel, a plain `Number`, from 0 (black) to 255
(white) by convention.
declarations.title: Gray

children.comments: A gray pixel is its one color channel.
children.title: <anonymous>

children.comments: Red, green and blue; alpha stays as it is.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A pixel type whose color channels can be mapped one by one, leaving
any other channel as it is: what converting a pixel between stored
values and light needs (`Puregrain.Gamma.toLight` and `fromLight`),
since alpha isn't on a light curve. Laws, as for `MapChannels`:

```purescript
mapColorChannels identity == identity
mapColorChannels (f <<< g) == mapColorChannels f <<< mapColorChannels g
```
declarations.title: ColorChannels

children.comments:
A gray pixel is its one channel: `perChannel` on `Number` is the
quantizer itself.
children.title: <anonymous>

children.comments:
Alpha too, like the other channels, as in the `Ring` and `Scalable`
instances.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A pixel type whose channels can be mapped one by one: what
`Puregrain.Quantize.perChannel` needs to run a one-channel quantizer
on every channel. Laws, as for any functor-like mapping:

```purescript
mapChannels identity == identity
mapChannels (f <<< g) == mapChannels f <<< mapChannels g
```
declarations.title: MapChannels

declarations.comments:
A pixel type that error diffusion can scale by a kernel's weights.
With `Ring`, for adding and subtracting error, it's what `ditherImage`
needs from a pixel type.
declarations.title: Scalable

declarations.comments:
A quantizer: picks a pixel's output value; `a` is the pixel type.
Build one with `quantize`, or `quantizeWith` when the decision depends
on the pixel's position; run one with `runQuantize`. Opaque, so its
representation can change without breaking anyone.

It gets the pixel's corrected value, with the error diffused into it
already added, and must be total: accumulated error pushes values
beyond the nominal range, below 0 or above 255, and the quantizer must
still return a sensible value. `ditherImage` diffuses the difference
between the corrected value and the output to the neighbours.
declarations.title: Quantize

declarations.comments:
Where the pixel being quantized sits: column `x` and row `y`, from 0
at the top-left. A record so it can grow, with a seed say, without
breaking quantizers: a helper that needs only some fields can take
`forall r. { x :: Int, y :: Int | r }`.
declarations.title: Context

declarations.comments:
The classic 1-bit quantizer: 0 (black) below the threshold, 255
(white) at or above it.

- `Number`: the threshold, usually 128.

`nearestLevel (evenRamp 2)` is the same with the cut fixed at 127.5.

With a gamma (`ditherImageWith`), the cut stays at the stored value:
it's converted to light once, so a gray below it still goes to black.
declarations.title: threshold

declarations.comments:
Runs a quantizer.

- `Quantize a`: the quantizer.
- `Context`: the pixel's position.
- `a`: the corrected value.

Returns the output value. For many pixels, apply it to the quantizer
once and keep the result, `let q = runQuantize quantizer`, then call
`q` for each pixel: some quantizers prepare things first.
declarations.title: runQuantize

declarations.comments:
A quantizer that also gets the pixel's position: ordered or noise
dithering, say, or a lookup in per-pixel data such as a mask.

- `Context -> a -> a`: from the position and the corrected value to
  the output value.

```purescript
-- 1-bit with the cut at 64 and 192 in a checkerboard
quantizeWith \{ x, y } v ->
  if v < (if (x + y) `mod` 2 == 0 then 64.0 else 192.0) then 0.0 else 255.0
```

With a gamma other than `gammaOff`, as for `quantize`: the function
still sees stored values, at two conversions per pixel.
declarations.title: quantizeWith

declarations.comments:
A quantizer that ignores the pixel's position, the common case.

- `a -> a`: from the corrected value to the output value.

```purescript
-- 1-bit with the cut at 100
quantize \v -> if v < 100.0 then 0.0 else 255.0
```

With a gamma other than `gammaOff` (`Puregrain.Dither.ditherImageWith`),
the function still gets and returns stored values: each pixel is
brought back from light before it and its result taken to light after,
while the error stays in light. That's two conversions per pixel; a
quantizer built with `quantizeInLight` needs none.
declarations.title: quantize

declarations.comments:
Runs a one-channel quantizer on every channel of a pixel,
independently, each with the pixel's position.

- `a`: the pixel type, with `MapChannels`: `Number`, `RGB` or `RGBA`.
- `Quantize Number`: the quantizer for one channel.

Dithering an RGB image this way gives exactly what dithering its three
channel planes separately would: a `Quantize Number` only ever sees
one channel, so it can't couple them. For a quantizer that looks at
the whole pixel, see `Puregrain.Palette.nearestColor`.

```purescript
-- 4 levels per channel
perChannel (nearestLevel (evenRamp 4)) :: Quantize RGB
```
declarations.title: perChannel

declarations.comments:
Snaps a value to the nearest of the given levels: the one-channel
sibling of `Puregrain.Palette.nearestColor`.

- `NonEmptyArray Number`: the levels, in any order; on an exact tie,
  the earlier wins.

Values below the lowest level snap to it, values above the highest to
that one.

```purescript
nearestLevel (evenRamp 4)   -- 0, 85, 170 or 255
```

With a gamma (`ditherImageWith`), a value still takes the level
nearest on stored values, while the error stays in light. Levels that
aren't whole numbers are rounded first (`evenRamp 3`'s 127.5 to 128),
so that every level comes back exactly.
declarations.title: nearestLevel

declarations.comments:
Evenly spaced levels from 0 to 255, both ends included, for
`nearestLevel`.

- `Int`: how many; 1 or less gives the single midpoint, 127.5.

`evenRamp 2 == [0.0, 255.0]`, `evenRamp 4 == [0.0, 85.0, 170.0, 255.0]`.
declarations.title: evenRamp

modules.comments:
Dithering with cells: the image is divided into cells of `width ×
height` pixels, and each cell may use only one or two colors, chosen
for it from a list of candidates. That's how the attribute cells of
8-bit home computers work, such as the ZX Spectrum's 8 × 8 cells with
an ink and a paper color (`Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum`). A
`CellMode` holds the cell size and the candidates; a machine module
exports one per screen mode. How it works and which rule suits which
picture: [docs/machine-screens/](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/machine-screens/README.md).

The image is processed in bands, one row of cells at a time. In each
band:

1. Every cell gets the candidate that fits its original pixels best.
   A candidate's score is the sum, over the cell's pixels, of each
   pixel's squared distance (in r, g and b) to the nearest color the
   candidate can produce: the nearest point on the segment between its
   two colors, since dithering can mix any share of them, or its one
   color. The lowest score wins; on a tie, the earlier candidate. A
   middle gray, for example, fits black and white perfectly, blue and
   white poorly.
2. The band's rows are dithered: a `CellQuantizer` turns each pixel
   into one of its cell's colors, and the kernel passes the error on,
   across cell and band borders.

`ditherCells` works on an image in memory, `ditherBands` on a lazy
stream of rows, with the same result:

```purescript
-- error diffusion inside the cells
ditherCells floydSteinberg nearestInCell mode image

-- pure ordered dithering inside the cells, with a threshold map m
ditherCells noDiffusion (orderedInCell m) mode image
```

`ditherCellsBy` and `ditherBandsBy` take their settings as a
`Puregrain.Dither.DitherParams` (the kernel, the gamma, …) in place of
the kernel; `ditherCellsWith` and `ditherBandsWith` take a `Gamma` from
`Puregrain.Gamma` and a kernel. Under a gamma the cells are the same,
with the rows dithered in light.

declarations.comments:
The size of a cell in pixels, for `CellMode`. A width or height below
1 counts as 1.
declarations.title: CellSize

declarations.comments:
The colors one cell may use: one color, or two that dithering mixes.
Build it with `singleColor` or `colorPair`. The order of two colors
doesn't change which cells choose them, nor what `nearestInCell`
gives; with `orderedInCell` it sets the pattern's direction.
declarations.title: CellPalette

declarations.comments: A cell palette of one color.
declarations.title: singleColor

declarations.comments:
A cell palette of two colors. The same color twice is a single color.

- `RGB`: the first color.
- `RGB`: the second color; the order matters only for
  `orderedInCell`.
declarations.title: colorPair

declarations.comments: The palette's colors: one, or two in the order they were given.
declarations.title: cellColors

declarations.comments:
A screen mode for cells: how big a cell is, and which palettes a cell
may use. A machine module exports one per screen mode, such as
`Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum.screen`.

- `c`: the candidate type, anything that stands for a cell's palette
  (for the ZX Spectrum, `Attribute`).
- `size`: the cell's width and height in pixels.
- `palette`: a candidate's colors.
- `candidates`: what a cell may use, in the order they're tried; on a
  tie the earlier wins.

For cells of your own, write the record; the candidates can be the
palettes themselves:

```purescript
mode :: CellMode CellPalette
mode =
  { size: { width: 4, height: 4 }
  , palette: identity
  , candidates: NEA.cons' (colorPair black white) [ colorPair blue yellow ]
  }
```

To change one part of a machine's mode, update its record, as in
`Zx.screen { candidates = fewer }`.
declarations.title: CellMode

declarations.comments:
How a pixel becomes one of its cell's colors. Build it with
`nearestInCell` or `orderedInCell`.
declarations.title: CellQuantizer

declarations.comments:
Each pixel becomes the nearer of its cell's colors, by squared RGB
distance (the first on a tie). With a kernel, that's error diffusion
inside the cells.
declarations.title: nearestInCell

declarations.comments:
Ordered dithering inside the cells. A pixel lies some fraction of the
way from its cell's first color to the second, measured along the
line between them; it becomes the second color where that fraction is
above the map's threshold at the pixel's position, else the first. A
single-color cell keeps its color.

- `ThresholdMap`: the thresholds, from `Puregrain.Ordered.bayer` or
  `compileThresholdMap`. Positions count from the image's corner, so
  any size works: a map whose side divides the cell's repeats in every
  cell, a larger one spreads more tone steps over several cells.

With `noDiffusion`, that's pure ordered dithering. With another kernel
it's the hybrid: the difference between a pixel's value and its color
is passed on.
declarations.title: orderedInCell

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory with cells, with the settings given.

- `c`: the mode's candidate type (see `CellMode`).
- `DitherParams`: the kernel, the gamma and the scan, from
  `Puregrain.Dither.defaults` and the `with…` functions.
- `CellQuantizer`: how each pixel picks one of its cell's colors.
- `CellMode c`: the cell size, and the candidates with their colors.
- `Array (Array RGB)`: the image, rows top to bottom, all of the same
  length.

Returns the candidate chosen for each cell, as rows of cells (top to
bottom, each left to right), and the dithered image. An image whose
size isn't a multiple of the cell size gets partial cells at the
right and bottom edges. Stops with an error naming a row whose length
differs from the first row's.

Under a gamma other than `gammaOff`, each cell's colors are still
chosen from the original pixels, as stored, so the cells are the same;
the band's rows are then dithered in light. `orderedInCell` measures
where a pixel lies between its cell's two colors in light;
`nearestInCell` still picks the nearer color on stored values, while
the error stays in light. When the cells' colors are whole numbers from
0 to 255, as a machine's are, every pixel comes out as exactly one of
its cell's colors, as a screen file needs.

```purescript
ditherCellsBy (defaults # withKernel atkinson) nearestInCell Zx.screen picture
```
declarations.title: ditherCellsBy

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory with cells, with a kernel and no other
setting.

- `c`, `CellQuantizer`, `CellMode c`, `Array (Array RGB)`: as for
  `ditherCellsBy`.
- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes; `noDiffusion` for nowhere.

Returns what `ditherCellsBy (defaults # withKernel kernel)` returns.
declarations.title: ditherCells

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory with cells, with a gamma and a kernel.

- `c`: as for `ditherCellsBy`.
- `Gamma`: how the stored numbers turn into light: `gammaOff`, the same
  as `ditherCells`, or a curve from `Puregrain.Gamma`.
- `Kernel`, `CellQuantizer`, `CellMode c`, `Array (Array RGB)`: as for
  `ditherCells`.

Returns what `ditherCellsBy (defaults # withKernel kernel # withGamma
gamma)` returns.
declarations.title: ditherCellsWith

declarations.comments:
Dithers a stream of rows with cells, one band (row of cells) at a
time, with the settings given.

- `c`, `DitherParams`, `CellQuantizer` and `CellMode c`: as for
  `ditherCellsBy`.
- `LL.List (Array RGB)`: the image as a lazy list of rows, top to
  bottom, all of the same length; it may be endless.

Returns a lazy list of bands, top to bottom, each with the candidates
chosen for its cells (left to right) and its dithered rows: the same
result as `ditherCellsBy`. A band's rows are read and dithered only when
the band is first needed, so only one band is in memory. When a band
holds a row whose length differs from the first row's, `ditherBands`
stops there with an error naming it; the bands before it have come out.
declarations.title: ditherBandsBy

declarations.comments:
Dithers a stream of rows with cells, one band at a time, with a kernel
and no other setting.

- `c`, `CellQuantizer`, `CellMode c`, `LL.List (Array RGB)`: as for
  `ditherBandsBy`.
- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes; `noDiffusion` for nowhere.

Returns what `ditherBandsBy (defaults # withKernel kernel)` returns.
declarations.title: ditherBands

declarations.comments:
Dithers a stream of rows with cells, one band at a time, with a gamma
and a kernel.

- `c` and `Gamma`: as for `ditherCellsWith`.
- `Kernel`, `CellQuantizer`, `CellMode c`, `LL.List (Array RGB)`: as for
  `ditherBands`.

Returns what `ditherBandsBy (defaults # withKernel kernel # withGamma
gamma)` returns.
declarations.title: ditherBandsWith

modules.name: Puregrain.Cells

modules.comments:
Dithering a whole image, in three ways that give the same rows for the
same input, with a kernel (`Puregrain.Kernel`) and a quantizer
(`Puregrain.Quantize`, `Puregrain.Palette`, `Puregrain.Ordered`):

- `ditherImage`: an image in memory, all at once;
- `ditherRows`: a lazy stream of rows, each dithered when it's needed;
- `initDithering` and `ditherRow`: one row at a time, with you running
  the loop. For rows that come from effects, such as a network stream
  or a file read piece by piece:

```purescript
-- readRow and writeRow are your own, here in Aff
loop :: Dithering Number -> Aff Unit
loop dithering = readRow >>= case _ of
  Nothing -> pure unit
  Just row -> case ditherRow dithering row of
    Left problem -> throwError (error problem)
    Right { row: dithered, next } -> writeRow dithered *> loop next

main = launchAff_ (loop (initDithering floydSteinberg (threshold 128.0)))
```

`Aff` keeps such a loop from growing the stack, however long the
stream; in `Effect`, write it with `tailRecM`.

Each takes its settings in one of two ways:

- `ditherImageBy`, `ditherRowsBy` and `initDitheringBy` take a
  `DitherParams`: the kernel, the gamma and the scan (`raster` or
  `serpentine`), built from `defaults` with the `with…` functions;
- `ditherImage`, `ditherRows` and `initDithering` take just a kernel,
  and their twins `ditherImageWith`, `ditherRowsWith` and
  `initDitheringWith` a `Puregrain.Gamma.Gamma` and a kernel: shorthands
  for the `…By` drivers with those settings.

```purescript
-- the same rows, twice
ditherImageBy (defaults # withKernel floydSteinberg # withGamma gammaSrgb) (threshold 128.0) image
ditherImageWith gammaSrgb floydSteinberg (threshold 128.0) image
```

A gamma keeps the amount of light, by that curve, rather than the
average of the stored numbers; `gammaOff` is the plain result. Which
gamma for which view:
[docs/gamma.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/gamma.md).

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory, with the settings given.

- `a`: the pixel type, `Number` for gray, `RGB` or `RGBA`; any type
  with `Ring`, `Scalable` and `ColorChannels` works.
- `DitherParams`: the kernel, the gamma and the scan, from `defaults`
  and the `with…` functions.
- `Quantize a`: picks each pixel's output value.
- `Array (Array a)`: the image, rows top to bottom, each left to right,
  all of the same length.

Returns the dithered image, all at once, as stored values. Under a
gamma other than `gammaOff`, each row is taken to light, dithered
there, and brought back: the error and the amounts of light (ordered
dithering's patterns) are in light; the choices of the nearest level
or color stay on stored values, as the eye sees them; a level or a
palette color of whole numbers comes back exactly. Stops with an error
naming a row whose length differs from the first row's.

```purescript
ditherImageBy (defaults # withKernel floydSteinberg # withGamma gammaSrgb) (threshold 128.0) image
```
declarations.title: ditherImageBy

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory, with a kernel and no other setting.

- `a`: the pixel type, `Number` for gray, `RGB` or `RGBA`; any type
  with `Ring` and `Scalable` works, `ColorChannels` not needed.
- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes; `noDiffusion` for nowhere.
- `Quantize a`: picks each pixel's output value.
- `Array (Array a)`: the image, as for `ditherImageBy`.

Returns what `ditherImageBy (defaults # withKernel kernel)` returns.
declarations.title: ditherImage

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory, with a gamma and a kernel.

- `a`: as for `ditherImageBy`.
- `Gamma`: how the stored numbers turn into light: `gammaOff`, the
  same as `ditherImage`, or `gamma1p2`, `gamma1p5`, `gamma1p8` or
  `gammaSrgb` (linear light).
- `Kernel`, `Quantize a`, `Array (Array a)`: as for `ditherImage`.

Returns what `ditherImageBy (defaults # withKernel kernel # withGamma
gamma)` returns.

```purescript
ditherImageWith gammaSrgb floydSteinberg (threshold 128.0) image
```
declarations.title: ditherImageWith

declarations.comments:
Dithers a lazy stream of rows, with the settings given.

- `a`, `DitherParams` and `Quantize a`: as for `ditherImageBy`.
- `LL.List (Array a)`: the rows, top to bottom, all of the same length;
  the list may be endless.

Returns the dithered rows as a lazy list, the same rows as
`ditherImageBy`. Each row is read and dithered only when its result is
first needed, so only the rows in flight are in memory. At a row whose
length differs from the first row's, it stops with an error naming
the row; the rows before it have come out.
declarations.title: ditherRowsBy

declarations.comments:
Dithers a lazy stream of rows, with a kernel and no other setting.

- `a`, `Kernel` and `Quantize a`: as for `ditherImage`.
- `LL.List (Array a)`: the rows, as for `ditherRowsBy`.

Returns what `ditherRowsBy (defaults # withKernel kernel)` returns.
declarations.title: ditherRows

declarations.comments:
Dithers a lazy stream of rows, with a gamma and a kernel.

- `a` and `Gamma`: as for `ditherImageWith`.
- `Kernel`, `Quantize a`, `LL.List (Array a)`: as for `ditherRows`.

Returns what `ditherRowsBy (defaults # withKernel kernel # withGamma
gamma)` returns.
declarations.title: ditherRowsWith

declarations.comments:
An image being dithered one row at a time, for `ditherRow`: the
settings, the quantizer, and the error waiting for the rows still to
come; `a` is the pixel type. Opaque.

An immutable value: keep and reuse one, for an undo, say. Dithering a
row from it again redoes that row's work, and no more.
declarations.title: Dithering

declarations.comments:
The state before the first row, for `ditherRow`, with the settings
given.

- `a`, `DitherParams` and `Quantize a`: as for `ditherImageBy`.

Dithers nothing yet; the first row fixes the image's width. `ditherRow`
then gives the same rows as `ditherImageBy`, each as stored values.
declarations.title: initDitheringBy

declarations.comments:
The state before the first row, for `ditherRow`, with a kernel and no
other setting.

- `Kernel` and `Quantize a`: as for `ditherImage`.

Returns what `initDitheringBy (defaults # withKernel kernel)` returns.
declarations.title: initDithering

declarations.comments:
The state before the first row, for `ditherRow`, with a gamma and a
kernel.

- `a` and `Gamma`: as for `ditherImageWith`.
- `Kernel` and `Quantize a`: as for `initDithering`.

Returns what `initDitheringBy (defaults # withKernel kernel # withGamma
gamma)` returns.
declarations.title: initDitheringWith

declarations.comments:
Dithers the next row.

- `Dithering a`: the state, from `initDitheringBy`, `initDithering`,
  `initDitheringWith` or the previous row.
- `Array a`: the row, as long as the first one.

Returns the dithered row and the state for the next one: the same rows
as the matching `ditherImage…`. `Left`, with a message naming the row,
for a row of a different length; the state passed in is untouched, so
you can carry on with a corrected row.
declarations.title: ditherRow

modules.name: Puregrain.Dither

declarations.comments:
The order the pixels are visited in, for `withScan`: `raster` or
`serpentine`. Opaque.
declarations.title: Scan

declarations.comments:
How an image is dithered, apart from the quantizer: the kernel, where
each pixel's error goes; the gamma, in which light; and the scan, the
order the pixels are visited in. Opaque: start from `defaults` and
change one setting at a time with the `with…` functions, chained with
`#`:

```purescript
params = defaults # withKernel floydSteinberg # withGamma gammaSrgb # withScan serpentine

dithered = ditherImageBy params (threshold 128.0) image
```

The order of the `with…` calls doesn't matter; a later call of the
same one replaces the earlier setting. The quantizer is an argument of
its own, since its type depends on the driver: a `Quantize a` for
`ditherImageBy`, a cell rule for `Puregrain.Cells.ditherCellsBy`.
declarations.title: DitherParams

declarations.comments:
Sets the scan, the order the pixels are visited in.

- `Scan`: `raster`, every row left to right (the default), or
  `serpentine`, the rows alternating.
- `DitherParams`: the settings to change.

Returns the settings with that scan, the others unchanged.
declarations.title: withScan

declarations.comments:
Sets the kernel.

- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes, from `Puregrain.Kernel`;
  `noDiffusion` for nowhere.
- `DitherParams`: the settings to change.

Returns the settings with that kernel, the others unchanged.
declarations.title: withKernel

declarations.comments:
Sets the gamma.

- `Gamma`: how the stored numbers turn into light, from
  `Puregrain.Gamma`: `gammaOff`, `gamma1p2`, `gamma1p5`, `gamma1p8` or
  `gammaSrgb`. Which for which view:
  [docs/gamma.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/gamma.md).
- `DitherParams`: the settings to change.

Returns the settings with that gamma, the others unchanged.
declarations.title: withGamma

declarations.comments:
Serpentine scanning: the rows alternate, the first (row 0) left to
right, the second right to left, and so on, top to bottom. On a row
scanned right to left the kernel is mirrored, so each pixel's error
still goes to pixels not yet processed: an offset's `dx` then counts
to the left. It's the usual remedy for the patterns error diffusion
draws when every row is scanned the same way.

Each pixel's quantizer still gets its own position, counted from the
image's left and top edges, so ordered dithering and machine cells
work as with `raster`. With `noDiffusion` it changes nothing. What it
changes, and what it doesn't:
[docs/error-diffusion.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/error-diffusion.md#serpentine-scanning).
declarations.title: serpentine

declarations.comments: Every row left to right, top to bottom: the default.
declarations.title: raster

declarations.comments:
The settings to start from, each one neutral: no diffusion
(`noDiffusion`), so each pixel is only quantized; `gammaOff`; and
`raster`, every row left to right. Dithering with them alone is plain
quantizing, or pure ordered dithering with a quantizer from
`Puregrain.Ordered`; add a kernel with `withKernel` for error
diffusion.
declarations.title: defaults

modules.comments:
How a picture's stored numbers turn into light, for dithering that keeps
the amount of light rather than the average of the numbers.

A gamma here doesn't adjust the picture, as an image editor's gamma
slider does: it says how the screen turns the numbers into light, and
the dithering then keeps that light. `gammaOff`, the default, converts
nothing, as dithering always has; `gammaSrgb` is linear light, the sRGB
standard's own curve; `gamma1p2`, `gamma1p5` and `gamma1p8` lie between.
Which value for which view, measured:
[docs/gamma.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/gamma.md).

The curves are computed from exact arithmetic only, so they give the
same results on every JavaScript engine; why and how:
[docs/exact-arithmetic.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/exact-arithmetic.md).

declarations.comments:
No conversion: the stored numbers are taken as amounts of light, as
dithering has always taken them. The default.
declarations.title: gammaOff

declarations.comments: A power curve: light = (value / 255)^1.2 × 255.
declarations.title: gamma1p2

declarations.comments: A power curve: light = (value / 255)^1.5 × 255.
declarations.title: gamma1p5

declarations.comments:
A power curve: light = (value / 255)^1.8 × 255, the gamma of Apple
RGB, the classic Macintosh's color space.
declarations.title: gamma1p8

declarations.comments:
Linear light: the sRGB standard's curve (IEC 61966-2-1), a straight
piece near black and a power of 2.4 above it, which behaves much like a
power of 2.2 overall.
declarations.title: gammaSrgb

declarations.comments:
Converts a pixel's color channels from stored values to light, on the
same 0–255 scale, leaving alpha as it is.

- `Gamma`: the curve.
- `a`: the pixel, as stored.

Returns the pixel in light. A whole number from 0 to 255 gets its light
from a table built once per curve, the first time it's needed; other
values from the curve's formula, with the same results. A negative
value gets the negative of its magnitude's light.

```purescript
toLight gammaSrgb 128.0   -- 55.04…, 21.6% of white's light
toLight gammaOff 128.0    -- 128.0
```
declarations.title: toLight

declarations.comments:
Converts a pixel's color channels from light back to stored values,
leaving alpha as it is.

- `Gamma`: the curve.
- `a`: the pixel, in light.

Returns the pixel as stored. The light of a whole number from 0 to 255
gives that number back exactly, so a palette's colors and a ramp's
levels come back as they were; other values go through the curve's
formula.

```purescript
fromLight gammaSrgb (toLight gammaSrgb 85.0)   -- 85.0, exactly
```
declarations.title: fromLight

declarations.comments:
A color's gray, for dithering a color picture in gray.

- `Gamma`: the curve, which decides the formula; give the dithering
  the same one.
- `RGB`: the color, as stored.

Returns the gray as a stored value, 0 to 255. A neutral color, with
red, green and blue equal, gives exactly that value. With `gammaOff`,
the gray is luma, 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B on the stored values, the
classic conversion. With a curve, it's the gray that gives off as much
light as the color: 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B on the channels'
light (luminance, with `gammaSrgb`), brought back to a stored value.
Saturated colors then come out lighter than with luma, pure blue 76
instead of 29 with `gammaSrgb`; natural colors such as skin barely
change.

```purescript
toGray gammaOff (RGB { r: 0.0, g: 0.0, b: 255.0 })    -- 29.07
toGray gammaSrgb (RGB { r: 0.0, g: 0.0, b: 255.0 })   -- 75.96…

ditherImageWith gammaSrgb floydSteinberg (threshold 128.0)
  (map (map (toGray gammaSrgb)) image)
```
declarations.title: toGray

modules.name: Puregrain.Gamma

declarations.comments:
A curve between a picture's stored values and light: one of
`Puregrain.Gamma`'s presets, `gammaOff`, `gamma1p2`, `gamma1p5`,
`gamma1p8` and `gammaSrgb`.
declarations.title: Gamma

modules.comments:
Fifth and cube roots from exact operations only (+, −, ×, ÷ and
comparisons), so that every JavaScript engine gives the same results:
ECMA-262 lets `Math.pow` and `Math.cbrt` differ between engines, but
not these operations. Internal: may change without notice.

Each root scales its input by exact powers of 2 into a small range,
[1/32, 1) for the fifth root and [1/8, 1) for the cube root, takes a
fixed number of Newton's steps from 1, and scales back. Scaling by
powers of 2 loses nothing, so the same number of steps fits every
input, from the smallest denormal up, and `fifthRoot (32.0 * x)` is
exactly `2.0 * fifthRoot x`.

The results are within two units in the last place of the nearest
number to the true root, mostly that number itself, so two neighbouring
inputs can get roots up to two units apart in either order. Why, how
often, and why it doesn't matter for dithering:
docs/exact-arithmetic.md.

declarations.comments:
The fifth root of any number. Odd: a negative number's root is the
negative of its magnitude's root. 0, the infinities and NaN come back
as they are.
declarations.title: fifthRoot

declarations.comments: The cube root of any number, as `fifthRoot` is the fifth.
declarations.title: cubeRoot

declarations.comments: One of Newton's steps towards the fifth root of `m`, from `y`.
declarations.title: fifthRootStep

declarations.comments: One of Newton's steps towards the cube root of `m`, from `y`.
declarations.title: cubeRootStep

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Exact

modules.comments:
The queues that carry error fractions from the pixel that produces
them to the pixel that receives them, and their implementations.
Internal: may change without notice.

children.comments:
`replicate n x` builds a `Fifo` containing exactly `n` copies of
`x`, in order — so `dequeue` on the result yields `x` exactly `n`
times before the `Fifo` becomes empty.

Called once per row, to build the leading zero-padding for an
offset with a positive `dx` (see `Puregrain.Internal.Kernel.paddingFor`), and
to build the leading zero-padding for the `current`/`building`
layers at the start of every row. `n` is always small — bounded
by the kernel's horizontal reach (its largest `dx`), never by image
width or height.

Target complexity: O(n). Since `n` is always small, this is never
the bottleneck regardless of the instance's constant factors.
children.title: replicate

children.comments:
`enqueue fifo x` appends `x` to the tail of `fifo`, returning the
extended `Fifo`. `fifo` itself is left unchanged — anyone still
holding a reference to it must keep seeing the original,
unextended contents (this is a pure, persistent operation, not a
mutation).

Called exactly once per pixel, for every offset with `dy == 0`
(`current`) and every offset with `dy > 0` (`building`). This is
the single hottest operation in the whole algorithm: its `O(n)`
cost on `Data.List.Lazy` — where `n` grows up to the image width
over the course of a row — is exactly what produced the
`O(width²)`-per-row, `O(width³)`-per-square-image blowup recorded
in `docs/benchmarks-fifo.md`.

Target complexity: O(1) amortized. An instance that can only
offer O(n) here reintroduces precisely the bug this class exists
to fix.
children.title: enqueue

children.comments:
`dequeue fifo` removes and returns the value at the head of
`fifo`, together with the remaining `Fifo` — or `Nothing` if
`fifo` is empty.

Called exactly once per pixel, for every offset being read this
row (`current` and `matured`). Together with `enqueue`, this
bounds the per-pixel cost of the whole algorithm.

`Nothing` is a real, expected outcome only when padding runs out
at the very edge of the image. `Puregrain.Internal.Step` treats any other
`Nothing` as a violated invariant and crashes loudly rather than
silently substituting a value — instances must not paper over
emptiness themselves (e.g. by returning a fabricated zero).

Target complexity: O(1) amortized.
children.title: dequeue

children.comments:
`replace skip fifo` drops the first `skip` elements from the
front of `fifo` and appends `skip` zeros to the tail, returning a
`Fifo` of the SAME LENGTH as the input — or, for an input shorter
than `skip`, of `skip` zeros, everything in it dropped (a row
narrower than the kernel's reach to the left). `skip` is always small
(bounded by the kernel's horizontal reach — see
`Puregrain.Internal.Kernel.skipFor`), but `fifo` itself may be as long as the
image width by the time this is called.

Called once per row, per offset with a negative `dx`, in
`Puregrain.Internal.Row.commitBuilding` — this re-aligns a fully-built row's
worth of error fractions with the next row's pixel positions
before it's handed off to its `DelayLine` slot.

This is its own method — rather than being left for callers to
express as "drop, then append a small replicated tail" — because
that composition is O(n) on a plain singly-linked list even
though `skip` is small (the append has to walk and rebuild the
entire dropped-and-kept prefix). An instance backed by a
structure with cheap concatenation (e.g. a finger tree, where
append is O(log(min(n1, n2)))) should implement `replace` using
that capability directly, to actually realize the better
complexity — not by delegating to `drop` + `<>`.

Target complexity: better than O(n) where the underlying
structure allows it. O(n) is acceptable only if the instance
genuinely cannot do better, and should be called out as a known
limitation in that instance's own documentation.
children.title: replace

children.comments:
`reverse fifo` holds the same elements in the opposite order: the
one at the tail comes out first.

Called once per row, per offset of a later row that is scanned in
the other direction (serpentine scanning), in
`Puregrain.Internal.Row.commitBuilding`: a finished queue holds its
error fractions in the order of the row that produced them, and the
row they're for reads them from its own end.

Target complexity: O(1) where the representation allows it. O(n)
is acceptable: it runs once per row, not per pixel, and the row's
own work is O(n) anyway.
children.title: reverse

children.comments:
Sanity-check baseline instance: this is the representation the
project used before `class Fifo` existed. `enqueue` and `replace`
are both O(n) here (a plain singly-linked list has no cheap way to
append at the tail) — an instance of `Fifo` using this should
reproduce the `O(N³)` scaling recorded for square images in
`docs/benchmarks-fifo.md`, not improve on it. Kept around specifically
to verify that the abstraction itself introduces no regression
relative to the pre-`class Fifo` code, and as a point of comparison
for the `CatQueue` instance below.
children.title: <anonymous>

children.comments:
The production default (`Puregrain.Internal.Image.ditherImage`). It replaced
`Data.Sequence.Seq`, the finger tree that first fixed the O(N³)
scaling (docs/benchmarks-fifo.md), on 2026-10-03: about 3.6× faster,
and a registry package instead of a git fork
(docs/benchmarks-dithering.md).

`Data.CatQueue` (package `catenable-lists`) is Okasaki's strict
two-list queue: a front list to dequeue from and a back list,
newest first, to enqueue onto. `enqueue` (`snoc`) is O(1).
`dequeue` (`uncons`) is O(1) amortized: when the front list runs
out, it reverses the back list once, in O(n). `replace skip` is
`skip` dequeues followed by `skip` enqueues of `zero`, so O(skip)
amortized, and `skip` is at most the kernel's reach. `replicate`
builds straight into the front list, so a fresh queue never needs
reversing. `reverse` swaps the two lists, in O(1): the queue is the
front list followed by the back list reversed, so the reversed queue
is the back list followed by the front list reversed. The old front
list, now the back, is reversed once when the new front runs out, as
any back list is, so the extra work is at most O(n) per row.

The amortized bounds hold only if each queue version is used once:
an old version used again would redo the same reversal. `step` and
`stepRow` use them that way, since every operation's result
replaces its input. Reusing a whole row's state (the public
`Dithering`) is fine: stepping from it again redoes that row's work,
the reversal included, and no more.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A FIFO-like container of `Number`s, used to hold error-diffusion
fractions for a single kernel offset as they travel from the pixel
that produced them to the pixel that consumes them.

Every method below is called exactly once per pixel (or once per
row, where noted) in the dithering hot path, so the real-world
performance of the whole algorithm is dominated by how cheaply an
instance can implement these five operations. Each instance should
document its own actual complexity per method, and should aim for
the target given here wherever its underlying representation
allows it — falling short of the target is not a correctness bug,
but it will show up directly in `docs/benchmarks-fifo.md`.
declarations.title: Fifo

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Fifo

modules.comments:
The light curves behind `Puregrain.Gamma`, on single values on the
0–255 scale. Internal: may change without notice. Why the curves are
built from exact operations only, and how: docs/exact-arithmetic.md.

declarations.comments:
A curve between a picture's stored values and light: one of
`Puregrain.Gamma`'s presets, `gammaOff`, `gamma1p2`, `gamma1p5`,
`gamma1p8` and `gammaSrgb`.
declarations.title: Gamma

declarations.comments:
What a driver hands a quantizer: a pixel type's two conversions, and
the curve itself, for quantizers of single channels (`perChannel`).
declarations.title: Conversion

declarations.comments:
No conversion, for `gammaOff`: the drivers and the quantizers check
`isOff` once per run and then skip converting altogether, so the
identities here are never called per pixel.
declarations.title: noConversion

declarations.comments: The conversion of a pixel type's color channels by a curve.
declarations.title: conversionFor

declarations.comments: Whether the curve is `Off`, the identity.
declarations.title: isOff

declarations.comments:
A curve from its two formulas on the 0–1 scale, defined for 0 and up:
scaled to 0–255 and mirrored for negative values, f(-v) = -f(v), as the
W3C's sample code (CSS Color 4) extends sRGB's.
declarations.title: curve

declarations.comments:
sRGB's curve (IEC 61966-2-1): a straight piece near black, then a
power of 2.4 with an offset. x^2.4 = x² · (⁵√x)²; back,
L^(5/12) = √√L · √∛L.
declarations.title: srgb

declarations.comments:
A value's light: a byte's from the table, any other value's from the
formula (the table holds the formula's results, so both agree).
declarations.title: toLightValue

declarations.comments:
A light value back to a stored one, for what's written: the light of a
byte gives that byte exactly, found in the table; any other value goes
through the formula.
declarations.title: fromLightValue

declarations.comments: The formula to light, without the table.
declarations.title: toLightFormula

declarations.comments:
The formula back, without the table: for the self-check and the
tests. The dithering's comparisons use `fromLightValue`, table first,
so that a byte's light comes back as exactly that byte.
declarations.title: fromLightFormula

declarations.comments: The light of the 256 bytes; for `Off`, the bytes themselves.
declarations.title: lightTable

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Gamma

modules.comments:
The two drivers that run the diffusion over a whole image, row by row,
with any `Fifo` backend and any conversion to light: `ditherImageVia`
over an array of rows (all at once) and `ditherRowsVia` over a lazy
list of rows (each when asked for), both with the settings compiled
(`Puregrain.Internal.Params.compileParams`). Both drive the same `stepRow`, so
they give the same result; a row of a different length, a `Left` from
`stepRow`, becomes a runtime error here, since neither result type can
carry it.
Internal: `Puregrain.Dither` exports them with the production backend;
the tests use them to check every backend against a reference.

declarations.comments: An image in memory: a strict fold over the array of rows.
declarations.title: ditherImageVia

declarations.comments: A stream of rows: a lazy unfold over the list of rows.
declarations.title: ditherRowsVia

declarations.comments:
A row converted to light before it's dithered, or left as it is when
the conversion is off.
declarations.title: rowsIn

declarations.comments:
A dithered row converted back from light, or left as it is when the
conversion is off.
declarations.title: rowsOut

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Image

modules.comments:
The compiled form of a kernel, built once per image so the per-pixel
step doesn't filter the kernel again for every pixel (PureScript
shares nothing automatically). Internal: may change without notice.

declarations.comments:
Precomputed per kernel: the offsets in the current row, the offsets
of each later row grouped by `dy` (layer i holds those with
`dy == i + 1`), and the deepest `dy`. Built once by `compileKernel`,
then passed on as plain data through the row and step code.
declarations.title: CompiledKernel

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Kernel

modules.comments:
The settings every driver shares, behind `Puregrain.Dither`'s opaque
`DitherParams`, and their compiled form. Internal: may change without
notice.

(The doc comments below the module's are what Pursuit shows, through
`Puregrain.Dither`'s re-export.)

declarations.comments:
How an image is dithered, apart from the quantizer: the kernel, where
each pixel's error goes; the gamma, in which light; and the scan, the
order the pixels are visited in. Opaque: start from `defaults` and
change one setting at a time with the `with…` functions, chained with
`#`:

```purescript
params = defaults # withKernel floydSteinberg # withGamma gammaSrgb # withScan serpentine

dithered = ditherImageBy params (threshold 128.0) image
```

The order of the `with…` calls doesn't matter; a later call of the
same one replaces the earlier setting. The quantizer is an argument of
its own, since its type depends on the driver: a `Quantize a` for
`ditherImageBy`, a cell rule for `Puregrain.Cells.ditherCellsBy`.
declarations.title: DitherParams

declarations.comments:
The order the pixels are visited in, for `withScan`: `raster` or
`serpentine`. Opaque.
declarations.title: Scan

declarations.comments:
The settings to start from, each one neutral: no diffusion
(`noDiffusion`), so each pixel is only quantized; `gammaOff`; and
`raster`, every row left to right. Dithering with them alone is plain
quantizing, or pure ordered dithering with a quantizer from
`Puregrain.Ordered`; add a kernel with `withKernel` for error
diffusion.
declarations.title: defaults

declarations.comments:
Sets the kernel.

- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes, from `Puregrain.Kernel`;
  `noDiffusion` for nowhere.
- `DitherParams`: the settings to change.

Returns the settings with that kernel, the others unchanged.
declarations.title: withKernel

declarations.comments:
Sets the gamma.

- `Gamma`: how the stored numbers turn into light, from
  `Puregrain.Gamma`: `gammaOff`, `gamma1p2`, `gamma1p5`, `gamma1p8` or
  `gammaSrgb`. Which for which view:
  [docs/gamma.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/gamma.md).
- `DitherParams`: the settings to change.

Returns the settings with that gamma, the others unchanged.
declarations.title: withGamma

declarations.comments:
Sets the scan, the order the pixels are visited in.

- `Scan`: `raster`, every row left to right (the default), or
  `serpentine`, the rows alternating.
- `DitherParams`: the settings to change.

Returns the settings with that scan, the others unchanged.
declarations.title: withScan

declarations.comments: Every row left to right, top to bottom: the default.
declarations.title: raster

declarations.comments:
Serpentine scanning: the rows alternate, the first (row 0) left to
right, the second right to left, and so on, top to bottom. On a row
scanned right to left the kernel is mirrored, so each pixel's error
still goes to pixels not yet processed: an offset's `dx` then counts
to the left. It's the usual remedy for the patterns error diffusion
draws when every row is scanned the same way.

Each pixel's quantizer still gets its own position, counted from the
image's left and top edges, so ordered dithering and machine cells
work as with `raster`. With `noDiffusion` it changes nothing. What it
changes, and what it doesn't:
[docs/error-diffusion.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/error-diffusion.md#serpentine-scanning).
declarations.title: serpentine

declarations.comments: The gamma of the settings, for the drivers' conversion to light.
declarations.title: gammaOf

declarations.comments:
What the row code needs of the settings, compiled once per image: the
kernel's offsets sorted by row (`CompiledKernel`), and the scan. The
kernel's compiled form stays apart from the scan, since the scan isn't
a property of the kernel: the per-pixel `step` needs only the kernel.
declarations.title: CompiledParams

declarations.comments:
Whether row `y` (counted from 0, the image's top) is scanned right to
left. Not stored anywhere: every row works it out from its own index,
`DitherState.nextRow`, so it can't disagree with the `y` the quantizer
sees.
declarations.title: rightToLeft

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Params

modules.comments:
`Quantize`'s inside, for the drivers that resolve a quantizer once per
run. Internal: may change without notice. `Puregrain.Quantize`
re-exports the type, opaquely, with its constructors and runner.

declarations.comments:
A quantizer: picks a pixel's output value; `a` is the pixel type.
Build one with `quantize`, or `quantizeWith` when the decision depends
on the pixel's position; run one with `runQuantize`. Opaque, so its
representation can change without breaking anyone.

It gets the pixel's corrected value, with the error diffused into it
already added, and must be total: accumulated error pushes values
beyond the nominal range, below 0 or above 255, and the quantizer must
still return a sensible value. `ditherImage` diffuses the difference
between the corrected value and the output to the neighbours.
declarations.title: Quantize

declarations.comments:
Where the pixel being quantized sits: column `x` and row `y`, from 0
at the top-left. A record so it can grow, with a seed say, without
breaking quantizers: a helper that needs only some fields can take
`forall r. { x :: Int, y :: Int | r }`.
declarations.title: Context

declarations.comments: A quantizer resolved for one run: what the core calls for each pixel.
declarations.title: Quantizer

declarations.comments:
A quantizer resolved with the driver's conversion, once per run. Bind
the result and call it for every pixel: calling `quantizerFor` again
for each pixel would redo the quantizer's preparation each time, since
PureScript shares nothing by itself.
declarations.title: quantizerFor

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Quantize

modules.comments:
One row of the diffusion: the step for each pixel, then handing the
row's queues over to the rows below. Internal: may change without
notice.

A row runs left to right, or right to left under serpentine scanning
(`Puregrain.Internal.Params.rightToLeft`). The queues hold their error
fractions in the order of the row that produced them, so a queue for a
row that runs the other way is reversed when it's handed over
(`handOver`); with alternating rows, that's every queue for a row an
odd number of rows below.

declarations.comments:
Dithers one row and returns the state for the next one. States are
plain immutable values: stepping from an old one again (an undo, say)
redoes that row's work, the queues' list reversals included, and no
more.

Every row must be as long as the first one. A row of a different
length is a caller's bug: `Left` with a message naming the row,
rather than reading past the queued error or leaving it misaligned
for the rows below. The state isn't touched, so the caller can retry.

The quantizer comes resolved (`Puregrain.Internal.Quantize.quantizerFor`),
once per run by the caller, not once per row or pixel. The row's
direction comes from the scan and the row's index, `state.nextRow`.
declarations.title: stepRow

declarations.comments:
The other half of `stepRow`'s contract: its `Left` (a row of a
different length, a caller's bug) becomes a stop with the same
message. For the drivers whose result type can't carry an error:
`ditherImage` and `ditherRows` (`Puregrain.Internal.Image`), and
`ditherCells` and `ditherBands` (`Puregrain.Cells`).
declarations.title: orStop

declarations.comments:
Hands a finished row's queues over to the rows below: each later
row's layer joins the end of its delay line. `turns dy` says whether
the row `dy` below runs the other way.
declarations.title: commitBuilding

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Row

modules.comments:
The engine self-check's machinery: the fingerprint of the light curves
and its stored reference. Internal: may change without notice. What it
checks and why: docs/exact-arithmetic.md, "The engine self-check".

declarations.comments:
The result of `Puregrain.SelfCheck.checkEngine`: whether the
JavaScript engine computed the light curves exactly as the reference,
and if not, what differed.
declarations.title: EngineReport

declarations.comments: One curve's results in one direction, folded into a whole number.
declarations.title: Digest

declarations.comments:
Each computed curve's formulas, both ways, over fixed values and the
generator's, each folded into a digest, in `referenceDigests`' order.
Takes `unit` so that nothing is computed when the module loads.
declarations.title: fingerprint

declarations.comments:
The reference: the fingerprint as Node 22.14 computed it, the same in
Node 26.13, Chromium 156, Firefox 157 and WebKit 27.2 (2026-11-14). It
changes only when a curve changes on purpose, in the same commit and
with a CHANGELOG line, since every picture dithered with that curve
then changes too; never just to make a check pass.
declarations.title: referenceDigests

declarations.comments:
A problem for each curve under which a byte doesn't come back exactly
from its light, through the table: a check that needs no reference.
declarations.title: roundTripProblems

declarations.comments:
The report: the digests that differ from the reference, then the
other problems.
declarations.title: reportFor

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.SelfCheck

modules.comments:
The state the diffusion carries along: the queues of error fractions
waiting for later pixels. Internal: may change without notice.

declarations.comments:
One queue per kernel offset of one row: the error fractions on their
way to the pixels of a later row (or, for the current row's offsets,
to pixels further right).
declarations.title: RowLayer

declarations.comments:
The maturing `RowLayer`s for one `dy`. It starts padded with `dy`
copies of the empty `RowLayer` (`[]`): a placeholder that contributes
zero error for free (`sumErrors [] = zero`), with no special case in
the step. An `Array` rather than a queue: it's always short, at most
the kernel's `maxDepth`.
declarations.title: DelayLine

declarations.comments:
What crosses from one row to the next: the delay lines; the index of
the next row (`nextRow`, the `y` the quantizer will see), kept here
rather than passed in, so a caller stepping row by row can't pass a
wrong one; and the image's `width`, taken from the first row
(`Nothing` before it), which every later row must match.

A plain immutable value: stepping from an old state again (an undo,
say) redoes that row's work, the queues' list reversals included, and
no more (see the `CatQueue` instance in `Puregrain.Internal.Fifo`).
declarations.title: DitherState

declarations.comments:
Row-local state, rebuilt for every pixel. `x` is the image column of
the next pixel and `y` this row's index — carried here rather than
computed by an indexed traversal, because `step` rebuilds this record
per pixel anyway (no extra allocation), whereas `mapAccumLWithIndex`
on Array is a generic default with an extra pass per row. `xStep` is
how `x` moves: +1 on a row scanned left to right, −1 on one scanned
right to left (serpentine), where `x` starts at the right edge. The
queues work in scan order either way; only the quantizer sees columns.
declarations.title: RowState

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.State

modules.comments:
One pixel of the diffusion: add up the error arriving from earlier
pixels, quantize, and send the new error on to the queues.
The queues work in scan order: on a row scanned right to left
(serpentine), an offset's `dx` counts to the left, so the kernel is
mirrored without being touched. Internal: may change without notice.
modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Step

modules.comments: Small helpers. Internal: may change without notice.

declarations.comments:
Like `(..)`, but returns `[]` when `lo > hi` instead of PureScript's
native descending-range behaviour (`1 .. 0 == [1, 0]`, not `[]` —
unlike Haskell's `[1..0] == []`). This codebase always wants the
Haskell-like "empty when inverted" semantics: every call site
builds a range from 1 up to some count that is legitimately allowed
to be 0 (e.g. `maxDepth`), and expects zero elements in that case,
not a spurious 2-element descending array.
declarations.title: safeRange

declarations.comments: Whether the rows form a grid of exactly `width` × `height`.
declarations.title: isGrid

declarations.comments:
"width x height", or, for rows of different lengths, how many rows:
for a message about a grid of the wrong size.
declarations.title: sizeOf

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Util

modules.comments:
Error-diffusion kernels: where each pixel's quantization error goes,
and in what shares.

Use a ready-made kernel, or build your own from a list of offsets
with `fromOffsets`, which checks it. The ready-made ones:
`floydSteinberg`, `atkinson`, `jarvisJudiceNinke`, `stucki`, `burkes`,
the Sierras `sierra3`, `sierra2` and `sierraLite`, `fan`, `shiauFan`
and `shiauFan2`; `noDiffusion` for none. Each one's table, its source
and what it suits:
[docs/error-diffusion.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/error-diffusion.md).

declarations.comments:
One neighbour that gets a share of a pixel's error.

- `dx`: columns to the right; negative to the left. With serpentine
  scanning (`Puregrain.Dither.serpentine`), a row scanned right to
  left mirrors the kernel: `dx` then counts to the left.
- `dy`: rows down.
- `weight`: the share of the error.
declarations.title: Offset

declarations.comments:
A checked list of neighbours. Build one with `fromOffsets`, or use a
ready-made one. Opaque, so every kernel `ditherImage` gets is valid.
declarations.title: Kernel

declarations.comments:
Checks a list of offsets and makes it a kernel.

- `Array Offset`: the neighbours and their shares.

`Left` says which offset breaks which rule (offsets counted from 0):

- every offset must point to a pixel not yet processed, in row-by-row
  scan order: a later row (`dy > 0`), or the same row further right
  (`dy == 0`, `dx > 0`);
- every weight must be a finite number (not NaN or infinite);
- no two offsets may point to the same neighbour.

The weights usually add up to 1, but needn't: Atkinson's add up to
3/4 on purpose. An empty list is valid: it's `noDiffusion`.

```purescript
-- half of the error to the right, half down
fromOffsets [ { dx: 1, dy: 0, weight: 0.5 }, { dx: 0, dy: 1, weight: 0.5 } ]
```
declarations.title: fromOffsets

declarations.comments: The kernel's offsets, as given to `fromOffsets`.
declarations.title: offsets

declarations.comments: Floyd–Steinberg (1976): 4 neighbours, the classic.
declarations.title: floydSteinberg

declarations.comments:
Atkinson (Apple, 1980s): 6 neighbours over the next 2 rows, each
getting 1/8, so only 3/4 of the error is passed on: crisper and
higher in contrast, at the cost of detail in dark and light tones.
declarations.title: atkinson

declarations.comments:
Jarvis–Judice–Ninke (1976): 12 neighbours over the next 2 rows, for
the smoothest texture, at about 2.5 times Floyd–Steinberg's cost.
declarations.title: jarvisJudiceNinke

declarations.comments:
Stucki (Peter Stucki, IBM Zurich, 1981): 12 neighbours over the next 2
rows, like Jarvis–Judice–Ninke, with weights that give a clean, sharp
result.
declarations.title: stucki

declarations.comments:
Burkes (Daniel Burkes, 1988): Stucki without its last row, so 7
neighbours over the next row: a little less clean, at a lower cost.
declarations.title: burkes

declarations.comments:
Sierra 3 (Frankie Sierra, 1989–1990; also "Sierra" or "three-row
Sierra"): 10 neighbours over the next 2 rows, for results like
Jarvis–Judice–Ninke's with fewer neighbours.
declarations.title: sierra3

declarations.comments:
